header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:ed-floovg:dipl, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. notes.1214: The text's -ai verb endings (donai, trovai, porai) are third-person forms (dona, trova, porra). Line 1216: par desor, literally 'above'; taken as 'by'. Line 1224: aucubes, pavilions or large tents.
notes.737: Line 737: ce droit lor recevez, 'receive this justice from them', sense uncertain; the Saracens seem to be calling for a captive to be hanged. Line 740: vaz taken as viez, 'old'. Line 743: annez taken as 'yearly'.

nodes.text: “Ah! Lord Muhammad, take this justice on them;
they are at your mercy, whenever you wish to hang him.”
There was a Saracen there named Jacobé,
all old and all white-haired, for he had passed a hundred years.
He was well versed in the law of Muhammad,
and he knew about the stars and the course of the sea;
he delivered the sermons to them at the great yearly feasts
on the law of Muhammad and of Apollin their god,
how he came to earth to save the people.
“Barons,” says the wretch, “listen to me in this:
Muhammad our lord is very noble and valiant;
who betrayed my lord with very great treachery;
God, fair Lord, grant that vengeance be taken for it.”
He has dismounted by an olive tree.
A spring rises there that is clear and still;
there he took a herb that a physician had given him,
and anointed his body with it, his face and his chest:
his skin was blacker than boiled pitch.
Now he will be able to go about freely among the pagan people
and speak that language, of which he knows the mastery well;
Maudarant and Maudoire will not recognise him at all.
He passes tents and pavilions without drawing rein,
and found the emir; with him, from his empire,
